demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Akua had always taken pride in her work as an architect, meticulously designing buildings that were both functional and aesthetically pleasing. But on a fateful day two years ago, her attention to detail failed her, and she accidentally caused a serious injury to one of her colleagues on a construction site. The sound of the man's screams still echoed in her mind, and the smell of freshly poured concrete transported her back to that moment. As Akua tried to make sense of what had happened, she began to perform mental rituals to prevent similar disasters from occurring again. She would replay every detail of the incident in her head, rehashing what she could have done differently, convinced that if she just thought about it enough, she could somehow undo the past. These mental exercises brought her a fleeting sense of control, but they also left her feeling drained and preoccupied. Akua often found herself comparing her situation to others, reminding herself that it could have been worse – after all, the injured colleague had survived. But this downward comparison only seemed to fuel her self-blame rumination, as she dwelled on what she perceived as her own culpability. She became consumed by thoughts of "What if?" and "If only...", replaying every possible scenario in which she could have acted differently. At work, Akua's difficulty concentrating made it challenging for her to focus on even the simplest tasks. Her colleagues began to notice a change in her demeanor – she was easily startled by ordinary sounds like hammers striking metal or the hum of the air conditioning system. She would jump, her heart racing, as if she were still on that construction site. Even outside of work, Akua's hypervigilance persisted; she often reacted to benign situations as if she were in danger. Akua struggled to deliberately recall the details of the incident, but certain sensory cues could transport her back to that day with unsettling vividness. The taste of freshly brewed coffee reminded her of the thermos she had been holding just before the accident, while the sound of a car alarm or the rustling of papers could trigger auditory flashbacks – the cacophony of sounds from the construction site echoing in her mind. Akua couldn't shake off the feeling that she was somehow broken, unrecognizable to herself and others. She began to withdraw from social interactions, feeling isolated and set apart from friends and family. Even her husband noticed a change in her; Akua's usual sparkle had dimmed, replaced by an air of detachment. At times, she wondered if she would ever be able to return to the person she once was. Akua's self-comparison to others only exacerbated these feelings of inadequacy. She couldn't help but think that someone else – someone more competent, more attentive – wouldn't have gotten into this situation in the first place. As the weight of her perceived failures bore down on her, Akua realized she needed help to untangle the complex web of emotions and memories that had taken over her life. Akua's husband encouraged her to seek professional help, but it was a chance conversation with a close friend – who shared a similar experience of trauma and recovery – that finally prompted her to take action. With trepidation, Akua made an appointment with a therapist, hoping that together they could unravel the threads of her entangled emotions and memories.
